concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: This is the named concept: transferring WAL transactions into the database file.

concepts.name: Checkpoint modes
concepts.reason: PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE, and NOOP are distinct checkpoint behaviors documented for this operation.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpointing
concepts.reason: SQLite has configurable rules for when it initiates checkpoints automatically.

concepts.name: Checkpoint progress and reader interference
concepts.reason: Active readers can limit checkpoint progress and prevent the WAL from being reset.

concepts.name: WAL reset and recycling
concepts.reason: A completed checkpoint can allow SQLite to reuse the WAL from its beginning.

concepts.name: Checkpoint performance and durability
concepts.reason: Checkpoint frequency and sync operations affect read performance, write performance, and durability.

concepts.name: SQLite WAL reader concurrency
concepts.reason: Reader snapshots and concurrent reads are related WAL topics, not checkpointing child concepts.

concepts.name: SQLite WAL writer concurrency
concepts.reason: Writer serialization is a related WAL topic, not an internal checkpointing concept.

concepts.name: SQLite rollback journal
concepts.reason: The rollback journal is contrasted with WAL but is not a checkpointing child concept.

claims.text: A checkpoint transfers transactions appended in the WAL file back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: SQLite treats checkpointing as a primitive operation alongside reading and writing in WAL mode.
claims.quote: with a write-ahead log there are now three primitive operations: reading, writing, and checkpointing.

claims.text: PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers, then syncs the database if all log frames were checkpointed.
claims.quote: Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: PASSIVE mode never invokes the busy-handler callback and may leave a checkpoint unfinished when readers or writers are concurrent.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: FULL mode waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent snapshot, then checkpoints all frames and syncs the database.
claims.quote: It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file. This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: RESTART behaves like FULL and also waits until all readers use only the database file, so the next writer can restart the WAL from the beginning.
claims.quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning. Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts while it is pending, but does not impede readers.

claims.text: TRUNCATE behaves like RESTART and truncates the log file to zero bytes before a successful return.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: NOOP checkpoints zero frames and can be used to read log and checkpointed frame counts through output parameters.
claims.quote: The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE can be initiated only through sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2().
claims.quote: FULL and RESTART checkpoints try harder to run the checkpoint to completion and can only be initiated by a call to sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2().

claims.text: By default, SQLite automatically checkpoints when a commit makes the WAL at least 1000 pages, or when the last database connection closes.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint configures a checkpoint after a commit when the WAL has at least N frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing zero or a negative N to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Automatic checkpoints use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE .

claims.text: Registering a WAL hook replaces the automatic checkpoint callback configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers but must stop before a WAL page past any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: SQLite remembers checkpoint progress in the wal-index and resumes from that point on the next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: A long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.
claims.quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

claims.text: If overlapping readers ensure at least one reader is always active, no checkpoint can complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: After the WAL has been transferred into the database and synced, SQLite rewinds it when no readers use it.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: A normal checkpoint recycles the WAL by overwriting from the beginning instead of truncating it.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: When the last database connection closes, it checkpoints once and deletes the WAL and associated shared-memory file.
claims.quote: When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk.

claims.text: As the WAL grows, read performance declines, so regular checkpoints help maintain read performance by keeping the WAL small.
claims.quote: Hence, to maintain good read performance it is important to keep the WAL file size down by running checkpoints at regular intervals.

claims.text: A checkpoint must sync the WAL before transferring content and sync the database before resetting the WAL to avoid corruption after power loss or hard reboot.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: Checkpoints are slower than write transactions because they require syncs and more seeking.
claims.quote: These factors combine to make checkpoints slower than write transactions.

claims.text: Frequent checkpoints can improve average read performance, while infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost over more writes.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT. To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible

claims.text: With synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync operation.
claims.quote: with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation
